when: before the well was dug, and every year since
what: The landing digs its plaster clay at a cut bank where the river swings west below the ford, on the station bank outside its walls. It was the landing's cut before the Imperials came, and the station has never claimed it. The landing renews the clay of its walls every dry season, and its clay work is renewed the same way.

when: the years since the well was dug
what: The Imperials set the well's stone head and lining in the clay bank by the ford. The bank moves with every monsoon, and the lining cracks. Each dry season Livia Varinius re-mortars the cracks herself, with a trowel and a tub of mortar she keeps under the windlass cover. Everyone can see the well head is cracked; nobody at the station knows the lining has cracked and been mended every year. Livia believes a mason's proper new lining will hold where her mortar did not; the lining was Imperial masons' work from the start and has cracked every year since.

when: 5 Rain's Hand, 4E 201 (the ledger page), early this dry season
what: A new crack opens a finger wide from the coping down the lining, on the side that faces the ford, below the water line, beside the old mortar lines. Livia writes it in the station ledger in the old log's order (time, count, state).

Ford water seeps through the lining below ground, and fine silt with it. The morning bucket comes up with silt in the bottom, and the water tastes of the ford. Livia keeps the silt in a jar under the windlass cover, beside her trowel and mortar tub, to show a mason when one comes. She gives a dipper of the well's water to any traveller who has paid the stop.

Livia asks the landing to haul stone for a new lining. Signs-For-The-Cargo refuses. The landing does not build in stone, and it does not drink the well's water; its households draw from the well only to wash.

when: this season, before the ledger page
what: Each bank has always charged for its own half of the stop. Livia raises the station's charge from one drake to two for every traveller who stops, for the stop and its water, to pay a mason from Gideon to re-line the well in stone. She charges the landing's people nothing for water, as she always has.

when: a few days after t5, before 3 Rain's Hand
what: In answer, Signs-For-The-Cargo begins to charge walkers who wade the ford one drake a head; before, only carts on the raft paid. He says the ford was worked before the well was dug. Travellers ask Livia why the landing charges them again, and she writes that in the ledger too.

Some travellers who have paid at the station slip out at night along the station bank, past the clay cut, and wade the shallow tail of the river below the pool, out of the poler's sight, to dodge the landing's charge. They leave prints in the clay of the cut.

when: ten days before the player comes
what: A crocodile, drawn by the offal from the drying racks and the night waders, takes the deep pool under the cut. It comes up at Signs-For-The-Cargo while he digs plaster clay. He drops the clay basket at the cut and runs. Nobody has dug there since. The station house has no watch post and nobody at the station hunts, so the crocodile has been left alone.

when: now, late in the dry season
what: The rains are close. The landing must replaster its walls before them and has no clay. Takes-The-Short-Weight, who judges everything by its water and keeps a bucket of ford water by her door, told the poler the walkers' charge is wrong and is sending travellers to the crocodile; he would not hear it.

when: every dry season, and early this one
what: The poler's wife draws wash water at the well (the ledger page, 4 Rain's Hand). She has watched Livia at the coping with a trowel every dry season, and this season saw her lift the windlass cover and put silt in a jar. She told Takes-The-Short-Weight.
Ahzi-Tal, a Helstrom courier, lodges for one night. Reeh-Shaal, who pays for her bed in salt and travels the same road, sees that his satchel holds a sealed packet his ledger does not list.
Reeh-Shaal buys a length of rope from Tsono-Ra after the lodge has closed, saying she needs it to tie her pack.

Reeh-Shaal kills Ahzi-Tal at the stone lip, takes the satchel, ties the body's wrists and pins it with a grave-stake in the spring's throat under the Hist's roots, so it will not float up. She leaves the stake's face uncarved.
Haj-Tei finds the courier's bed empty, his pack still in the lodge store and his bill unpaid. He decides the courier left before dawn without paying and keeps the pack against the debt.
The body fouls the water. Guests who drink it, or eat food cooked in it, fall sick with fever and retching.
Reeh-Shaal stays at the lodge, saying she waits for a boat to Helstrom. She waits for the packet's buyer, who has not come, and tells the sick guests it is the fire stand's food.
After the lamps are out, Reeh-Shaal goes to the stone lip and looks down into the water for a while, to be sure the body has not come up.

In a dry year the founders went down the root galleries and cut a channel from a brine seam toward the roots of a rival grove downstream, to sour its water and take its travellers. The rival grove withered; Greenspring grew.
The founders carved the descent on their own grave-stakes in the old way, as a deed done for the tribe, and never spoke of it to outsiders.
With the grove downstream dead, the channel silted on that side; each flood now pushes the brine back up the cut into Greenspring's own taproots.
Vees-Wai finds the Hist's leaves falling out of season and the sap thin. The village tastes salt in the spring and blames the salt works upstream.
Ixo-Vaal stopped trading for salt-works salt when the works closed their landing; he now buys upriver rock salt, which he keeps in a sack at his door.
